title: Breakdown of Charge-Conjugation Symmetry of Disclinations in 2D Crystals
authors: Ruslan Yamaletdinov, Mikhail I. Katsnelson, Oleg V. Yazyev
abstract: Disclinations are elementary topological defects in two-dimensional (2D) crystalline membranes, yet their elastic properties remain largely unexplored. Using atomistic simulations, we address the energetics, morphology, and interactions of disclinations in free-standing graphene, a prototypical 2D crystal. We find that while disclinations with positive topological charges follow an expected behavior, negative disclinations exhibit sublinear energy scaling with charge as well as equilibrium shape that deviates sharply from the conventional saddle ansatz. This breakdown of charge-conjugation symmetry leads to qualitatively distinct interactions: positive disclinations repel, whereas negative disclinations display a robust long-range attraction. These trends are shown to be further amplified by self-adhesion in folded membranes. Our results uncover a fundamentally different energetic landscape for negative curvature defects and provide a basis for understanding the stability, self-folding behavior, and defect-driven morphology of graphene and other 2D membranes.
summary: This work explores the physics of topological defects (disclinations) in 2D crystals like graphene. Using simulations, the authors reveal that the elastic behavior of these defects is not symmetric with respect to the sign of their topological charge. Specifically, they find that negative defects interact attractively, contrasting sharply with the repulsive interactions observed for positive defects.
main_problem: The study investigates the elastic properties, energetics, and interactions of topological defects called disclinations in 2D crystalline membranes.
main_result: The paper finds a fundamental breakdown of charge-conjugation symmetry: positive disclinations repel, while negative disclinations exhibit a robust long-range attraction.
method: The research combines atomistic simulations with continuum elasticity theory to calculate the energy and morphology of disclination configurations.
model_or_system: The system is a free-standing 2D crystal, specifically graphene, containing topological defects (disclinations) characterized by a topological charge $s$. The analysis compares theoretical continuum predictions with atomistic simulation results.
key_observables: Interaction energy ($E_{exc}$), energy scaling with charge $|s|$, equilibrium shape, and adhesion energy in folded membranes.
important_parameters: Topological charge ($s$), bending rigidity ($\kappa$), and separation distance ($\Delta r$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on continuum models, such as the saddle ansatz, and uses approximations like the four-cone configuration to model negative curvature defects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction of positive and negative disclinations, compare energy fits showing deviations from expected scaling for negative charges, and show how self-adhesion stabilizes negative curvature defects.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using continuum elasticity, then uses atomistic simulations to test the theory for positive and negative charges, culminating in a detailed comparison of interaction forces and the role of self-adhesion.
why_interesting: While the topic is condensed matter physics, the study of topological defects and symmetry breaking in low-dimensional systems shares conceptual links with defect physics in quantum materials or engineered quantum structures.
